h1: Prototype vs. Production: When Should You Change the Manufacturing Process?

headings.text: Prototype vs. Production: When Should You Change the Manufacturing Process?
Why Is CNC or 3D Printing Usually Right for Prototypes?
Why Does Injection Molding Take Over at Higher Volumes?
How Do You Know When You’ve Crossed the Threshold?
What Happens If You Switch Processes Too Early or Too Late?

images.alt: Prototype and production manufacturing with CNC machined, 3D printed and injection molded parts

meta_description: Learn when CNC machining or 3D printing makes sense for prototypes and when injection molding becomes more cost-effective for production.
monitored_text: Prototype vs. Production: When Should You Change the Manufacturing Process? by eMachineShop | Sep 18, 2026 « Back to all posts The process that’s right for one prototype is often the wrong process for 5,000 units — and the reverse is just as true. Knowing when to switch is a cost decision, not a maturity milestone. Quick summary: CNC machining and 3D printing dominate prototyping because they require no tooling investment. Injection molding and other tooled processes dominate production because per-unit cost drops dramatically once tooling is amortized — but only past a volume threshold that justifies the tooling cost. Why Is CNC or 3D Printing Usually Right for Prototypes? No tooling investment. You can iterate a design multiple times without paying for a mold each time you change a feature. Why Does Injection Molding Take Over at Higher Volumes? Mold tooling is expensive upfront, but the per-unit cost afterward is very low. Past a certain volume, that trade pays for itself — often faster than most people expect. How Do You Know When You’ve Crossed the Threshold? Compare total cost at your expected volume: CNC/3D print cost scales roughly linearly per unit; injection molding has a large fixed cost plus a low variable cost. The crossover point depends on part complexity and material, but it’s a calculable number, not a guess. What Happens If You Switch Processes Too Early or Too Late? Switching to tooling too early risks paying for a mold before the design is finalized — expensive if it changes. Staying on CNC too long into production means paying a higher per-unit cost indefinitely. FAQ Can a design go straight from sketch to injection molding, skipping CNC prototyping? Technically yes, but it’s risky — any design flaw discovered after the mold is cut is expensive to fix. Is there a hybrid approach? Yes — some programs use CNC-machined “bridge tooling” to produce a few hundred units while production tooling is still being built.
